articles.title: Karson, keep the two stops. Fix everything that made you need them.
articles.dek: Sunyshore held Blackthorn to 17 rushing yards and still needed two late defensive answers. Mara Voss sees an excellent front—and a warning behind it.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I would hang the final two defensive answers in Sunyshore's meeting room. I would also put the 368 passing yards right beside them, in lettering large enough to ruin everybody's breakfast. Karson Jones has an 8–2 team because his defense made the necessary plays against Blackthorn. That is a reason to trust the Starseekers under pressure. It is a terrible reason to stop asking how much pressure they volunteered to absorb.

At 2:20 of the fourth quarter, Marowak sacked Hatterene on the two-point attempt that could have tied the game. At 1:14, Serp Gardener stopped Seadra after nine yards on fourth-and-eleven. Sunyshore won 21–20. Those are different problems solved by different defenders: get to the passer before the try develops, then make a tackle before the receiver reaches the sticks. Both deserve to be remembered exactly, without being melted into a vague compliment about wanting it more.

The final possession is the better teaching sequence. Exploud caught an eleven-yard pass to start it. Furret then lost a yard running up the middle against Don Philliams. Hatterene missed deep left, Ash Rothington broke up the deep-right throw, and Serp Gardener finished the fourth-down play two yards short. Sunyshore made Blackthorn play the entire series. Nobody needed a spectacular interception to end it. A failed run, two unsuccessful passes and a disciplined tackle did the work.

I like that. I particularly like the tackle. We spend so much time celebrating the ball in the air that a defender who understands where the first down lives can disappear from the discussion. Seadra caught the pass. Serp Gardener still won the down. There is no contradiction in those two facts, and there should be no confusion about which one mattered with a one-point lead.

But go back to the larger afternoon. Hatterene completed 28 of 42 passes for 368 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions. Sawsbuck caught six for 142. Exploud caught ten of eleven targets for 94. That is sustained access to a defense, not a couple of freak completions we can wave away while admiring the final scoreboard. The Dragons gained 385 total yards and sixteen first downs. Sunyshore gave itself too many difficult conversations.

The ground defense was excellent. Blackthorn managed seventeen yards on thirteen rushing attempts. Furret had twenty-one on eight carries; the remaining attempts pulled the team total down. Jones's front made running a poor answer for most of the game. Sunyshore has allowed only 365 rushing yards through ten games, so this was consistent with an established strength. I am not asking the Starseekers to abandon that strength. I am asking them to stop treating it as the solution to every question.

Look at the distribution. Exploud's ten receptions kept producing manageable gains, while Sawsbuck supplied the larger chunks. If you only worry about the deep receiver, the underneath catches can extend a drive. If you only squeeze the underneath work, the larger completion changes the field. I cannot tell you the private instructions on any defender's wristband. I can tell you that Blackthorn found productive answers at more than one depth and that those answers survived well into the fourth quarter.

The offense gave the defense considerable help, then less of it. FLOAT SZN ran for 146 yards and two touchdowns on twelve carries. The seventy-yard run up the middle with thirty-seven seconds left in the second quarter was the kind of play that can make an entire game plan look wiser than it felt one snap earlier. He had lost a fumble on Sunyshore's opening play. Jones kept getting him involved, and the back answered. That part of the afternoon deserves applause without a footnote.

"I wanted the next carry to be useful to everybody," FLOAT SZN said. "The line didn't stop working because I lost one. I couldn't either." That is the right-sized answer. A seventy-yard touchdown makes an excellent apology. The more useful part is continuing to do the job after the mistake, because nobody gets to schedule when the long run arrives.

After Jolt Vick's three-yard touchdown catch made the lead 21–7 in the third quarter, the Starseekers never scored again. They finished two-for-eight on third down and punted five times. Blackthorn scored twice in the fourth. Even after the failed tying try, Sunyshore could not finish the game with its offense: an eleven-yard run earned a first down, but an incompletion, a three-yard run and a five-yard run brought another punt. The defense had to go back out and solve the problem again.

That is the part I would put on Jones's desk. There is a perfectly understandable temptation to describe every narrow road win as playoff preparation. Sometimes it is. Sometimes your defense is practicing emergency repairs because your offense has stopped making first downs. DeZhaun Watzon protected the ball, throwing no interceptions, but 175 passing yards and two third-down conversions left little room for a quiet finish. The running game's spectacular moment did not supply an endless supply of possessions.

"We made the stops we needed," Jones said. "I'd rather learn from a win, but the last series doesn't erase the ones before it." Good. Keep that sentence. The coach does not need to apologize for beating an 8–2 opponent on the road, and I am not asking him to. I want the corrections to receive the same attention as the relief. A contender should be capable of celebrating and studying in the same building.

Eterna comes next. The Thorns just lost 38–0, which makes them an easy opponent to underestimate and a useful test of Sunyshore's patience. The Starseekers do not need to manufacture another dramatic fourth quarter to prove they can win one. They need to turn their defensive advantage into enough ordinary offensive possessions that the final drive belongs to their own kneeling quarterback. If Eterna struggles to move the ball, keep making it struggle; do not hand it a shorter route back into the game.

I believe in this defense's ability to make a hard stop. Marowak and Serp Gardener gave me two very good reasons. I also believe Jones has enough evidence to demand a cleaner afternoon. Freeze the last fourth-down catch on the screen: Seadra has the ball, Serp Gardener has the tackle, and the first-down line is still two yards away. Keep that frame. Then rewind.

art.alt: Sunyshore’s late defensive boundary and the passing routes that tested it.

articles.title: Petalburg would like its lead back in the conversation
articles.dek: Rustboro gets the unbeaten visitor. Petalburg has the division lead. Ellis Quill thinks the distinction deserves a little attention.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: There is a pleasant kind of anonymity available to a team that keeps winning while someone else gets the interesting visitor. Petalburg is 7–3, leading Hoenn West, and preparing for Sootopolis. Rustboro is 6–4 and preparing for unbeaten Mossdeep. I know which game people will talk about first. I would like to spend a few minutes with the team that is already in front.

Norman's Pride won 24–17 at Pewter without producing a passing line anyone will frame. Iron Valiant completed fourteen of twenty-five throws for 115 yards. There were two touchdowns and no interceptions, which is a much better description of his afternoon than the yardage alone. Petalburg rushed for 145 yards, recovered a fumble and made the long field goal that left the home team with too much to do. The victory was assembled from useful pieces.

Oinkologne supplied two of the most useful. On fourth-and-two in the third quarter, he caught a two-yard touchdown pass. Early in the fourth, he ran up the middle for a one-yard score. A receiving touchdown of two yards and a rushing touchdown of one are not likely to win a contest for the week's most beautiful highlights. They were, however, exactly the distances Petalburg needed. I have a soft spot for players who decline to make a simple assignment sound inadequate.

"If it's two yards, I'll take two," Oinkologne said. "We can admire the long ones after we finish the short ones." There is a brave little impatience in that answer. He carried fifteen times for seventy yards, so the afternoon was not all short work. But those two scoring plays explain the Pride's approach better than a grand statement about identity ever could. Find the job, finish the job, let someone else count the style points.

The fourth-down touchdown was followed almost immediately by Pewter's fumble. Sandslash recovered it for Petalburg. It is tempting to treat those moments as luck lining up politely for the visitors, but a team has to convert the opening. The Pride turned the next possession into Oinkologne's one-yard score. In a game decided by seven points, the ability to make the next opportunity useful was the difference between controlling the afternoon and merely participating in it.

Pewter still made the finish uncomfortable. There was an eight-yard fourth-down touchdown pass to Marowak, and later a two-yard fourth-down scoring pass to Cranidos with eighteen seconds remaining. Before that last drive, Sunflora had made a fifty-three-yard field goal at 1:56. That kick gave Petalburg a fourteen-point cushion. By the time Cranidos scored, the Rockers needed an onside recovery as well as another touchdown. Cradily recovered the kick for the Pride. Iron Valiant took a knee.

I mention the sequence because narrow final scores can flatten the story. Petalburg did not spend the final eighteen seconds trying to prevent one ordinary possession from becoming a tying touchdown. The Pride had already made Pewter spend most of the remaining time on its first necessary score. The onside kick was a real danger, and Cradily still had to secure it. But the long field goal had changed the demands on the opponent. That is what a good kick buys.

"You don't want to need every one of those details," Norman said. "You do want everyone to understand that their detail counts." He has a team with a plus-thirty-four point differential, not the sort of margin that encourages leisurely afternoons. Petalburg has scored 186 points and allowed 152. Seven wins have come from that narrower space. I would be careful about assuming the Pride can always live there, and equally careful about dismissing a team that has repeatedly found a way through it.

The comparison with Rustboro is interesting because the Stone have produced more noise in fewer winning afternoons. Their most recent game was a 41–38 victory over Cinnabar before the Week 11 bye. They have scored 205 points and allowed 174, almost the same overall differential as Petalburg despite the different shape of the results. Rustboro can make a game feel open and urgent. Petalburg just won with 115 passing yards and a very important fifty-three-yard kick. Both routes count.

Dewford is also 6–4 after winning 16–10 at Celadon. That makes the division lead a live responsibility rather than a comfortable possession. Petalburg cannot outsource its Week 12 work to Mossdeep, however useful a Rustboro defeat might look from a distance. Sootopolis has four wins and just lost at Fuchsia. The Surge have also shown they can put together a clean passing game when allowed to settle. Norman's team needs to win its own afternoon before admiring the result from Rustboro.

I resist calling this a statement game for the Pride. Everything is a statement game once we run out of more specific language. Petalburg's statement is the record it has already built. Week 12 is an opportunity to preserve a one-game lead over two pursuers and to keep a division winner's route through the postseason within its own reach. That is plenty. We do not need to pretend a comfortable spot has been secured, or that the next loss would erase ten weeks of work.

Iron Valiant was characteristically economical about the attention. "The backs gave us places to go," he said. "The line kept giving us another down. I'm happy if the numbers tell that part too." His two touchdown passes traveled to Delcatty and Oinkologne for short scores. There is no need to inflate them into feats they were not. The quarterback put the ball where a small gain could become six points. Some afternoons, that is the whole brief.

The Pride's lead also gives the next several weeks a different emotional rhythm. Chasing teams can spend a good deal of time imagining what one win might repair. A team in front has to keep doing the unglamorous work that made the lead possible. Norman will not get to protect first place with an explanation of why Rustboro's matchup received more attention. He gets Sootopolis, a fresh opening kickoff, and the same obligation to make the next manageable play.

I will watch Mossdeep at Rustboro with everybody else. It deserves the attention. I will also keep an eye on Petalburg, because the Hoenn West standings still begin with the Pride. Last week their final necessary touch belonged to Cradily on an onside kick. A player secured the ball, a quarterback knelt, and the division leader went home with its seventh win.

art.alt: Oinkologne and Iron Valiant approach Petalburg’s stadium through a leafy park.

articles.title: Koga, do not let 2–9 become an excuse
articles.dek: Fuchsia finally paired Empoleon’s passing with protection and a defense that finished. Dorian Pike demands that the Shadows remember the recipe.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Koga, I have a modest request. Keep the tape. Label it clearly. Put it somewhere nobody can mistake it for a souvenir from a season that has already disappointed them. Fuchsia beat Sootopolis 24–14, and for once the Shadows gave their quarterback an afternoon in which every completed pass did not appear to be negotiating with disaster. Empoleon threw for 283 yards. He took no sacks. He threw no interceptions. I would like those three facts to become acquainted with one another permanently.

Yes, Fuchsia is 2–9. I can read the standings. I have been reading them while this team found creative ways to make good passing yardage feel like an apology. Empoleon now has 2,427 passing yards. A quarterback can accumulate a large number while his team loses; nobody needs another seminar on that point. What matters is whether the rest of the operation gives those yards somewhere useful to go. This week, it did.

The Shadows gained 382 total yards, made seventeen first downs and allowed only six. They held the opposing ground game to thirty yards on eleven attempts. They recorded three sacks and an interception. They won by ten despite missing two field goals and losing a fumble. This was not a perfect performance that briefly appeared from a more successful team's wardrobe. It was an imperfect performance with enough competent football underneath it to survive its own mistakes.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: a 2–9 team still has standards to meet. The record does not issue an exemption. It makes the demand more urgent. If Koga can get this protection, this level of quarterback efficiency and this much defensive resistance in the same game, then I want to know why the next opponent should be allowed to treat Fuchsia as a pleasant stop on the schedule. I am finished congratulating opponents for showing up.

Start with Vivillon. Six catches, 122 yards, two touchdowns. There was also a fumble after a twenty-five-yard catch late in the second quarter. That detail stays in the column. I am not polishing the evidence until it reflects a nicer team. The important response came after halftime: a twenty-nine-yard touchdown catch, then a five-yard touchdown catch, both to the left. Fuchsia continued to throw to a player who could hurt the defense. The player rewarded the decision.

"I wanted another chance with the ball," Vivillon said. "Two touchdowns felt a lot better than spending the whole evening talking about the one I dropped." Good. Enjoy them. Then remember that the first mistake did not force the coaching staff to abandon the receiver, and the receiver did not force the quarterback to stop trusting him. A young season can be full of promises. An eleven-game season needs useful responses. Those two catches were useful.

Empoleon completed twenty of twenty-seven passes. Heatmor caught six of seven targets for seventy-seven yards. Gumshoos caught all four of his for thirty-three. The distribution matters because the offense was not reduced to begging one player for another rescue. Vivillon had the largest afternoon, but there were other catches available and other receivers finishing their assignments. A defense asked to respect several productive routes has more work to do than one waiting for the same desperation throw.

The protection deserves its own paragraph, and it is getting one. Zero sacks. I am writing that again because quarterbacks on losing teams are so often discussed as if every dropback happens in a private room. Empoleon had been sacked twenty-four times across the season's recorded totals; none came in this game. Whatever compliments go to the passer should leave enough room for the players who prevented the pocket from becoming an emergency exit. That is a collective achievement.

Fuchsia also ran the ball thirty-one times for ninety-nine yards. Oinkologne supplied eighty-five on twenty-one carries. Bibarel scored from a yard out in the first quarter. I am not going to sell 3.2 yards per team rushing attempt as a revelation. I am going to recognize that the Shadows could keep calling runs without asking the quarterback to solve every down by himself. Bibarel's touchdown was a one-yard answer to a one-yard problem. Those answers have been in short supply.

Now the defense. Cacturne and Sharpedo each sacked the opposing quarterback for seven-yard losses, and Gumshoos added another sack. Seaking intercepted a deep-left throw. Seven passes were swatted away. The opponent completed eleven of twenty-seven attempts and converted two of ten third downs. You can build a winning afternoon around that kind of resistance. You cannot spend the following week acting surprised that resistance was permitted.

The ending was even better than the big defensive totals. After Fuchsia missed a forty-yard field goal at 1:58, the opponent still had a small opening. A nine-yard completion created second-and-one. Then came an incompletion, a run for no gain stopped by Sharpedo, and a fourth-down run that lost a yard to Cacturne. At 1:46, Empoleon began taking knees. The defense closed the door after the kicker had failed to do it. That is what a team is supposed to be for.

"We didn't have to ask for the ball back," Koga said. "We had to finish the down in front of us." Fine. Keep that answer too. There is a temptation around a losing club to describe every good moment as a preview of next season. I object. There are games left in this season. There are players trying to establish that their work should matter now. Fuchsia's defense did not stop that fourth-down run for the benefit of a future slogan.

Pewter is next, and I expect Fuchsia to arrive with an actual plan to win. That is not a claim that the Shadows have suddenly become a contender. It is a refusal to let nine losses lower the standard for the next opportunity to do something useful. Repeat the protection. Keep multiple receivers involved. Make the opponent earn its third downs. If the field-goal unit leaves points behind, do not allow the rest of the team to use the miss as permission to drift.

Koga, the record is bad. The football does not have to stay bad. Your quarterback finished this game with 283 passing yards and no sacks, and your defense finished it by denying one yard twice. Put those two plays on the first screen at the next meeting. Leave them there long enough for everybody to read the distance.

art.alt: Empoleon prepares to throw from a spacious purple pocket.
